Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: From Systemic Inflammation to Calcium Leak: The RyR2 Hypothesis of Reversible Myocardial Dysfunction in Andes Virus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome
papers.abstract: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) caused by Andes virus is a severe zoonotic disease characterized by a paradoxical cardiac phenotype: profound myocardial dysfunction that is frequently reversible in survivors and occurs without extensive structural damage. The mechanisms linking systemic inflammation to this reversible dysfunction remain unknown. This review examines the hypothesis that inflammatory signaling converges on the cardiac ryanodine receptor (RyR2), a major intracellular Ca2+-release channel, through post-translational modifications, generating reversible myocardial dysfunction in HCPS. In severe disease, elevated IL-6, reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, and nitrosative stress activate pathways that in experimental models converge on RyR2 through CaMKII-dependent phosphorylation at Ser2814, oxidative modification of cysteine residues, and S-nitrosylation, each destabilizing the channel and promoting diastolic Ca2+ leak. The resulting increase in spontaneous Ca2+ release reduces SR Ca2+ content, impairs contractility, and predisposes to arrhythmias. This framework identifies RyR2 as a plausible mechanistic hub for the reversible cardiac phenotype. Therapeutic implications are discussed, emphasizing the timing of interventions and the potential of rycals, drugs that stabilize the closed state of RyR2 and prevent diastolic Ca2+ leak, as an emerging strategy. This model provides a testable hypothesis for a disease that currently lacks specific treatment.

analysis.background: Andes virus–induced hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) causes severe, often reversible myocardial dysfunction without extensive structural damage (A1).
analysis.main_directions: The review links systemic inflammation (elevated IL‑6, ROS, nitrosative stress) to post‑translational modifications of the cardiac RyR2 channel—CaMKII‑dependent phosphorylation, oxidative cysteine alteration, and S‑nitrosylation—producing diastolic Ca2+ leak and arrhythmogenic risk (A4).
analysis.current_state: RyR2 is identified as a plausible mechanistic hub that integrates inflammatory signals to generate reversible cardiac dysfunction, summarizing existing experimental data (A3, A6).
analysis.gaps: The exact molecular cascade connecting systemic inflammation to RyR2 dysfunction in HCPS remains unproven (A2).
analysis.future_research: Testing RyR2‑stabilizing drugs (rycals), clarifying optimal timing of intervention, and experimentally validating the RyR2 hypothesis in HCPS patients are proposed (A7, A8).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes virus HCPS causes severe but often reversible myocardial dysfunction without major structural damage (A1). Main directions: Systemic inflammation (IL‑6, ROS, nitrosative stress) modifies RyR2 via CaMKII phosphorylation, oxidative cysteine changes, and S‑nitrosylation, leading to diastolic Ca2+ leak and arrhythmia risk (A4). Current state: RyR2 is presented as a plausible hub linking inflammation to reversible cardiac failure, based on existing experimental evidence (A3, A6). Gaps: The precise pathways linking inflammation to RyR2 dysfunction remain unproven (A2). Future research: Testing RyR2‑stabilizing agents (rycals), defining optimal treatment timing, and validating the hypothesis in HCPS patients are recommended (A7, A8).

papers.title: Hantavirus emergence through a One Health lens: ecological dynamics, human exposure and integrated surveillance
papers.abstract: Abstract Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonotic viruses that cause haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in the Americas. Although human hantavirus infections are usually recognised clinically, infection risk is affected by upstream factors including reservoir-host ecology, environmental variability and human exposure. Evidence from China, Europe and the Americas shows that the incidence of hantavirus may depend on rodent population dynamics, climate conditions, land use, agricultural practices, housing environments and recreational or travel-related exposure. In China, the seasonal pattern of haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, including a major autumn–winter peak and a smaller spring or spring–summer peak in many endemic areas, illustrates how virus–host ecology and agricultural labour jointly affect the human risk. In Europe, bank vole population cycles have been shown to influence Puumala virus epidemics, while studies in the Americas have linked rainfall, rodent abundance and human exposure in domestic, occupational and recreational settings. This mini review synthesises evidence on the ecological drivers, exposure pathways and surveillance challenges for hantavirus diseases through a One Health lens. We suggest that One Health approaches should move beyond general calls for multisector collaboration towards evidence-informed surveillance linking rodent, environmental and human data to setting-specific prevention, such as issuing seasonal risk warnings and reinforcing exposure-reduction measures before harvest periods in endemic agricultural regions.

Hantavirus emergence through a One Health lens: ecological dynamics, human exposure and integrated surveillance Xinyu Wang1,2* Abstract Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonotic viruses that cause haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in the Americas. Although human hantavirus infections are usually recognised clinically, infection risk is affected by upstream factors including reservoir-host ecology, environmental variability and human exposure. Evidence from China, Europe and the Americas shows that the incidence of hantavi- rus may depend on rodent population dynamics, climate conditions, land use, agricultural practices, housing environ- ments and recreational or travel-related exposure. In China, the seasonal pattern of haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, including a major autumn–winter peak and a smaller spring or spring–summer peak in many endemic areas, illustrates how virus–host ecology and agricultural labour jointly affect the human risk. In Europe, bank vole population cycles have been shown to influence Puumala virus epidemics, while studies in the Americas have linked rainfall, rodent abundance and human exposure in domestic, occupational and recreational settings. This mini review synthesises evidence on the ecological drivers, exposure pathways and surveillance challenges for hantavirus diseases through a One Health lens. We suggest that One Health approaches should move beyond general calls for multisec- tor collaboration towards evidence-informed surveillance linking rodent, environmental and human data to setting- specific prevention, such as issuing seasonal risk warnings and reinforcing exposure-reduction measures before har- vest periods in endemic agricultural regions. Keywords Hantavirus, One Health, Haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, Rodent reservoir, Ecological surveillance, China, Travel medicine Introduction The epidemiology of hantaviruses is tightly linked to res- ervoir hosts, environmental conditions and human expo- sure, making them a useful model for reviewing zoonotic emergence through a One Health lens. Medically impor- tant hantaviruses are maintained primarily in rodent reservoirs and are associated with two major human disease syndromes: haemorrhagic fever with renal syn- drome (HFRS), reported mainly in Europe and Asia, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS; also his- torically referred to as hantavirus pulmonary syndrome), reported mainly in the Americas [1–3]. Human infec- tion is usually accidental and occurs when people enter environments contaminated by infectious rodent excreta; however, Andes virus remains the major exception, with documented person-to-person transmission under con- ditions of close or prolonged contact [3, 4]. Rather than cataloguing hantavirus species, this review focuses on synthesising the evidence for how ecological *Correspondence: Xinyu Wang snowmed@gmail.com 1 Department of Infectious Diseases, Huashan Hospital, Fudan University, Shanghai 200040, China 2 National Medical Center for Infectious Diseases, Shanghai 200040, China Page 2 of 7 Wang ﻿One Health Advances (2026) 4:36 and social processes shape human infection. Key ques- tions are not only which virus is carried by which rodent, but under what environmental and behavioural condi- tions infected reservoirs and susceptible humans are brought into contact. This framing is relevant for the One Health approach, because hantavirus risk can be exam- ined across measurable links including the rodent popu- lation density, reservoir-infection prevalence, climate variability, land use, agricultural or occupational expo- sure, housing conditions, recreational travel and clinical surveillance [1, 5]. China’s long-standing HFRS experi- ence, Europe’s cyclic Puumala virus epidemics and HCPS outbreaks in the Americas collectively provide comple- mentary evidence for understanding hantavirus emer- gence as an integrated human–animal–environment problem. This makes hantavirus disease a useful case for examining how the One Health approach can move from a conceptual framework to measurable surveillance indi- cators and setting-specific prevention. Reservoir ecology and environmental drivers of hantavirus risk The geographic distribution of hantavirus infection is strongly affected by its reservoir-host ecology. Although an increasing variety of hantaviruses have been detected in mammals, medically important hantaviruses are mainly maintained in rodent reservoirs, and many patho- genic viruses show close associations with particular host species or host complexes [1, 2]. This host dependence helps to explain the geographically uneven hantavirus risk, with human disease only occurring where compe- tent reservoirs, suitable habitats and human exposure all overlap. However, reservoir presence alone is insuf- ficient to predict human risk, and the local incidence also depends on rodent abundance, infection prevalence within reservoir populations, seasonal movement, habi- tat disturbance and the frequency with which humans enter contaminated environments [5]. Environmental variability can influence hantavirus transmission by changing the reservoir-host population dynamics and human–rodent contact. Increased rain- fall may enhance vegetation growth and food availabil- ity for rodents, thus supporting their reproduction and survival, while drought, habitat disruption or cold stress may drive rodents into human dwellings, storage areas or workplaces. The Four Corners region of the southwestern United States remains a classic example, where El Niño- associated precipitation led to ecological conditions that favoured increases in deer mouse populations, with a subsequent marked increase in HCPS cases in affected areas [6]. In Europe, Puumala virus epidemics have been linked to bank vole population cycles influenced by for- est ecology, food availability and seasonal conditions [7]. These examples suggest that climate is not a direct cause in isolation, but can influence risk via reservoir ecology and exposure pathways. Because human hantavirus cases often occur after changes in reservoir populations, rodent abundance and infection prevalence can act as early-warning indicators. Long-term ecological studies in Europe and the Americas have shown that rodent population cycles may precede changes in human disease risk [6, 7]. In China, ecologi- cal studies of HFRS have also emphasised the interacting roles of environmental variability, reservoir ecology and human behaviour in shaping disease dynamics [5]. These findings support a practical One Health implication: rodent monitoring should not be treated solely as ecolog- ical research, but as part of an integrated risk-assessment system linking animal, environmental and human health data. Land use, agriculture and human exposure: evidence from China and beyond Land use determines how often reservoir hosts, con- taminated environments and susceptible humans share the same space. Agricultural expansion, crop harvesting, grain storage, peri-domestic farming structures, forest edges and poorly sealed rural housing can increase the opportunities for contact with rodent excreta. A system- atic review of land cover, land use and human hantavi- rus infection risk found that agricultural land use was positively associated with infection risk in several set- tings, particularly in China and Brazil, whereas associa- tions with forest cover, grassland or built-up areas varied by region and virus ecology [8]. This heterogeneity is important, in that land use is not a universal risk factor but rather modifies exposure through local combinations of reservoir species, farming systems, housing conditions and human behaviour. China provides one of the clearest examples of how virus ecology and human activity jointly structure hanta- virus seasonality. In many endemic areas, HFRS shows a bimodal pattern, with a larger autumn–winter peak and a smaller spring or spring–summer peak. In China, this bimodal pattern has often been interpreted as reflect- ing the coexistence of different virus–host systems and exposure settings. Hantaan virus, mainly associated with Apodemus agrarius, contributes more to field or rural exposure and autumn–winter incidence, whereas Seoul virus, carried by Rattus norvegicus, is more relevant to peri-domestic or urban transmission and spring inci- dence in many settings [9–11]. In Zibo City, HFRS cases peaked during March–May and October–December, illustrating the seasonal human risk pattern [9]. Spatial analyses from the same region further suggested that Page 3 of 7 Wang ﻿One Health Advances (2026) 4:36 spring and autumn risks differed geographically, support- ing targeted seasonal prevention [12]. The link between agricultural activity and HFRS sea- sonality is particularly evident in high-incidence prov- inces such as Shandong. A time-series analysis reported marked seasonality and discussed the temporal cor- respondence between agricultural activity and HFRS incidence: the autumn harvest usually begins in late September, cases then rise rapidly in October, peak in November, and decline in December [13]. The incubation period of hantavirus infection suggests that this pattern is biologically plausible and consistent with exposure dur- ing harvesting, field work, grain handling or temporary accommodation in rodent-infested settings. Together with the smaller spring peak observed in many endemic areas, this pattern suggests that HFRS risk is shaped by seasonally changing combinations of reservoir ecology, agricultural labour and peri-domestic exposure, rather than by a single constant pathway. In addition to agriculture, hantavirus exposure may occur in occupational, domestic, recreational and travel settings. Farmers, forestry workers, construction work- ers, cleaners, military personnel and people entering rodent-infested buildings may experience intense short- term exposure when contaminated dust is disturbed. Recreational exposure can occur when visitors stay in cabins, campsites or enclosed structures with rodent infestation. The 2012 Yosemite National Park outbreak, linked to overnight stays in insulated tent cabins, showed how built environments can convert local rodent ecology into visitor risk [14]. The 2026 cruise-associated Andes virus cluster illustrates a different pathway, with local ecological exposure potentially becoming a multi-coun- try public health problem when combined with delayed recognition, confined travel settings and international movements [15]. Surveillance evidence and gaps across human– animal–environment systems China’s long-term HFRS experience provides an instruc- tive example of surveillance that already contains several One Health elements, even if not always labelled as such. National surveillance has combined human case report- ing with rodent surveillance, laboratory testing and tar- geted prevention in endemic areas. During 2006–2012, 77,558 HFRS cases and 866 deaths were reported in China. Cases were clustered in a small number of prov- inces and occurring mainly in spring and autumn–win- ter seasons, with farmers remaining the largest affected occupational group [10]. More recent national data for 2014–2023 show continuing geographic and virological complexity, with Hantaan virus, Seoul virus and Puu- mala virus among the identified human HFRS-associated hantaviruses in China [11]. These regional contrasts are summarised in Table 1, which compares rodent, envi- ronmental and human surveillance components across China, Europe and the Americas. Despite the value of long-term case reporting, human surveillance alone is inherently too late for hantavirus prevention, and human cases usually only appear after ecological changes, rodent population shifts and expo- sure events have already occurred. Clinical recogni- tion may also be delayed because the early symptoms are non-specific and overlap with leptospirosis, dengue, influenza-like illness, malaria, COVID-19 and other febrile syndromes [3]. This is particularly relevant in rural or travel-related settings, where the exposure event may be remote in time and place from the diagnosis. For surveillance to support prevention rather than only documentation, clinical signals should be connected with rodent, environmental and exposure information. In clinical practice, a compatible syndrome combined with a carefully reconstructed exposure history—such as recent rural residence, crop harvesting, cleaning of rodent-infested spaces, cabin stay or expedition travel— may provide the first actionable signal before laboratory confirmation. The One Health challenge is therefore not simply to collect more data, but to link the appropriate data to timely decisions. Information on rodent density, reser- voir infection prevalence, climate anomalies, agricultural calendars, land-use changes, clinical syndromes and travel or occupational histories is often held by different sectors and interpreted separately. Broader One Health early-warning literature emphasises the importance of bottom-up reporting and grassroots actors for reduc- ing delays between outbreak emergence, notification and response [16]. For hantavirus diseases, integrated early warning should therefore be judged not by the number of assembled datasets, but by whether ecological and clinical signals lead to earlier, setting-specific preven- tion. Future surveillance should therefore be built around predefined risk questions and response thresholds rather than around parallel human, animal and environmental datasets. In resource-limited settings, integrated One Health surveillance should not aim to monitor every possible ecological, animal and human indicator. A more feasible approach is to develop a minimum surveillance package tailored to local risk settings, combining routine report- ing of compatible human syndromes, simple rodent-den- sity indicators, seasonal agricultural calendars, rainfall or flooding alerts, community reports of rodent infestation and exposure histories collected during clinical assess- ment. Sentinel surveillance sites in high-risk counties, farms, storage facilities or travel destinations may be a Page 4 of 7 Wang ﻿One Health Advances (2026) 4:36 Table 1 Comparative One Health surveillance components for hantavirus diseases in China, Europe, and the Americas ANDV Andes virus; HCPS hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome; HFRS haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome; HTNV Hantaan virus; PUUV Puumala virus; SEOV Seoul virus; SNV Sin Nombre virus Region Disease pattern Rodent signal Environmental signal Human exposure Operational implication China/HFRS Bimodal seasonality; major autumn–winter and smaller spring peaks Apodemus agrarius/HTNV; Rattus norvegicus/SEOV; rodent density and infection prevalence Agricultural seasons, land use, rural/peri-domestic environments Farmers, harvest, planting, grain storage, rural housing Seasonal warnings and targeted prevention around agricultural activities Europe/PUUV Cyclic epidemic years Bank vole population dynamics Forest ecology, masting, seasonal food availability Rural residents, forestry/recrea- tional exposure Rodent and ecological monitoring may support early warning Americas/HCPS and ANDV Sporadic severe HCPS; ANDV person-to- person transmission exception Deer mouse/SNV; Oligoryzomys longicaudatus/ANDV Rainfall anomalies, vegetation pulses, regional reservoir habitats Domestic/cabin exposure, expedition travel, close contacts for ANDV Combine ecological exposure assessment with clinical recognition and contact monitoring Page 5 of 7 Wang ﻿One Health Advances (2026) 4:36 more sustainable approach than broader, continuous sur- veillance. Standardised metrics could include monthly rodent density, the proportion of captured rodents test- ing positive, rainfall deviation from the seasonal baseline, the number of compatible human cases, the proportion with documented exposure history and the number of high-risk settings receiving seasonal risk communication. Institutional coordination could be organised through periodic joint risk assessment meetings involving public health, clinical, agricultural, veterinary, environmental and travel or tourism sectors, with each warning signal linked to predefined prevention measures. Figure 1 illus- trates this proposed framework by linking ecological early-warning indicators to clinical decision nodes and public health actions. Prevention and preparedness: recent progress and remaining gaps Given the absence of widely licensed vaccines or specific antiviral therapies for most hantavirus diseases, preven- tion still relies primarily on reducing exposure to infected rodents and their excreta. Measures such as rodent- proofing buildings, safe grain storage, environmental san- itation, wet disinfection before cleaning and avoidance of dust-generating activities in infested spaces are well established and docum…

Hantavirus emergence through a One Health lens: ecological dynamics, human exposure and integrated surveillance Xinyu Wang1,2* Abstract Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonotic viruses that cause haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in the Americas. Although human hantavirus infections are usually recognised clinically, infection risk is affected by upstream factors including reservoir-host ecology, environmental variability and human exposure. Evidence from China, Europe and the Americas shows that the incidence of hantavi- rus may depend on rodent population dynamics, climate conditions, land use, agricultural practices, housing environ- ments and recreational or travel-related exposure. In China, the seasonal pattern of haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, including a major autumn–winter peak and a smaller spring or spring–summer peak in many endemic areas, illustrates how virus–host ecology and agricultural labour jointly affect the human risk. In Europe, bank vole population cycles have been shown to influence Puumala virus epidemics, while studies in the Americas have linked rainfall, rodent abundance and human exposure in domestic, occupational and recreational settings. This mini review synthesises evidence on the ecological drivers, exposure pathways and surveillance challenges for hantavirus diseases through a One Health lens. We suggest that One Health approaches should move beyond general calls for multisec- tor collaboration towards evidence-informed surveillance linking rodent, environmental and human data to setting- specific prevention, such as issuing seasonal risk warnings and reinforcing exposure-reduction measures before har- vest periods in endemic agricultural regions. Keywords Hantavirus, One Health, Haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, Rodent reservoir, Ecological surveillance, China, Travel medicine Introduction The epidemiology of hantaviruses is tightly linked to res- ervoir hosts, environmental conditions and human expo- sure, making them a useful model for reviewing zoonotic emergence through a One Health lens. Medically impor- tant hantaviruses are maintained primarily in rodent reservoirs and are associated with two major human disease syndromes: haemorrhagic fever with renal syn- drome (HFRS), reported mainly in Europe and Asia, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS; also his- torically referred to as hantavirus pulmonary syndrome), reported mainly in the Americas [1–3]. Human infec- tion is usually accidental and occurs when people enter environments contaminated by infectious rodent excreta; however, Andes virus remains the major exception, with documented person-to-person transmission under con- ditions of close or prolonged contact [3, 4]. Rather than cataloguing hantavirus species, this review focuses on synthesising the evidence for how ecological *Correspondence: Xinyu Wang snowmed@gmail.com 1 Department of Infectious Diseases, Huashan Hospital, Fudan University, Shanghai 200040, China 2 National Medical Center for Infectious Diseases, Shanghai 200040, China Page 2 of 7 Wang ﻿One Health Advances (2026) 4:36 and social processes shape human infection. Key ques- tions are not only which virus is carried by which rodent, but under what environmental and behavioural condi- tions infected reservoirs and susceptible humans are brought into contact. This framing is relevant for the One Health approach, because hantavirus risk can be exam- ined across measurable links including the rodent popu- lation density, reservoir-infection prevalence, climate variability, land use, agricultural or occupational expo- sure, housing conditions, recreational travel and clinical surveillance [1, 5]. China’s long-standing HFRS experi- ence, Europe’s cyclic Puumala virus epidemics and HCPS outbreaks in the Americas collectively provide comple- mentary evidence for understanding hantavirus emer- gence as an integrated human–animal–environment problem. This makes hantavirus disease a useful case for examining how the One Health approach can move from a conceptual framework to measurable surveillance indi- cators and setting-specific prevention. Reservoir ecology and environmental drivers of hantavirus risk The geographic distribution of hantavirus infection is strongly affected by its reservoir-host ecology. Although an increasing variety of hantaviruses have been detected in mammals, medically important hantaviruses are mainly maintained in rodent reservoirs, and many patho- genic viruses show close associations with particular host species or host complexes [1, 2]. This host dependence helps to explain the geographically uneven hantavirus risk, with human disease only occurring where compe- tent reservoirs, suitable habitats and human exposure all overlap. However, reservoir presence alone is insuf- ficient to predict human risk, and the local incidence also depends on rodent abundance, infection prevalence within reservoir populations, seasonal movement, habi- tat disturbance and the frequency with which humans enter contaminated environments [5]. Environmental variability can influence hantavirus transmission by changing the reservoir-host population dynamics and human–rodent contact. Increased rain- fall may enhance vegetation growth and food availabil- ity for rodents, thus supporting their reproduction and survival, while drought, habitat disruption or cold stress may drive rodents into human dwellings, storage areas or workplaces. The Four Corners region of the southwestern United States remains a classic example, where El Niño- associated precipitation led to ecological conditions that favoured increases in deer mouse populations, with a subsequent marked increase in HCPS cases in affected areas [6]. In Europe, Puumala virus epidemics have been linked to bank vole population cycles influenced by for- est ecology, food availability and seasonal conditions [7]. These examples suggest that climate is not a direct cause in isolation, but can influence risk via reservoir ecology and exposure pathways. Because human hantavirus cases often occur after changes in reservoir populations, rodent abundance and infection prevalence can act as early-warning indicators. Long-term ecological studies in Europe and the Americas have shown that rodent population cycles may precede changes in human disease risk [6, 7]. In China, ecologi- cal studies of HFRS have also emphasised the interacting roles of environmental variability, reservoir ecology and human behaviour in shaping disease dynamics [5]. These findings support a practical One Health implication: rodent monitoring should not be treated solely as ecolog- ical research, but as part of an integrated risk-assessment system linking animal, environmental and human health data. analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic viruses causing HFRS in Eurasia and HCPS in the Americas, posing a public‑health threat. Methods: This mini review synthesises evidence on ecological drivers, exposure pathways and surveillance challenges through a One Health lens. Results: Data from China, Europe and the Americas indicate that incidence is linked to rodent dynamics, climate, land use, agriculture, housing and travel exposure; seasonal patterns in China and vole cycles in Europe show joint host‑human effects; Americas studies connect rainfall, rodent abundance and exposure settings to cases. Contribution: The review urges evidence‑informed, integrated surveillance linking animal, environmental and human data for setting‑specific prevention, e.g., seasonal warnings and pre‑harvest measures. Limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒 是啮齿动物传播的动物源性病毒,可导致欧亚地区的肾综合征出血热,以及美洲的 汉坦病毒心肺综合征,构成显著的公共卫生关注。
analysis_zh.methods: 本小型综述通过一体化健康视角综合已发表的证据,探讨了汉坦病毒疾病的生态驱动因素、暴露途径和监测挑战。
analysis_zh.results: 来自中国、欧洲和美洲的证据表明,汉坦病毒发病率取决于啮齿动物种群动态、气候条件、土地利用、农业实践、住房环境以及休闲或旅行相关暴露;中国的季节性模式和欧洲的银行田鼠周期说明宿主生态与人类活动共同影响风险;美洲的研究将降雨、啮齿动物丰度和多样化暴露环境与人类病例联系起来。
analysis_zh.contribution: 作者提出超越一般多部门合作,推动以证据为依据的综合监测,将啮齿动物、环境和人类数据关联,以实现针对特定场景的预防措施,如季节性风险预警和收获前暴露降低措施。
analysis_zh.limitations: 在提供的证据中未报告。

papers.title: Human Orthohantavirus infections: From virology and clinical epidemiology to oral biological features and dental practice
papers.abstract: Abstract Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonotic pathogens responsible for 2 severe clinical syndromes in humans: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), affecting an estimated 150,000 to 200,000 individuals annually worldwide, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), characterized by fulminant pulmonary edema with case fatality rates approaching 40%. Although the systemic manifestations of hantavirus disease are well described, the oral and salivary dimensions of infection have received comparatively little attention in the dental literature. This review synthesizes current evidence on the virology, global epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, oral complications, diagnostic approaches, treatment options, and dental practice implications of human hantavirus infections. A narrative review with a structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar was conducted, supplemented by hand-searching and by consultation of the World Health Organization and European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control outbreak reporting. Particular attention was directed toward primary research on salivary immunity, oral fluid diagnostics, and salivary gland tropism. Andes virus (ANDV) antigen has been detected in secretory cells of human salivary glands, and ANDV uniquely resists the antiviral capacity of human saliva, providing a biologically plausible mechanism for its person-to-person transmissibility. Infectious virus has since been recovered from saliva and gingival crevicular fluid during acute infection, although a salivary route of transmission remains an epidemiological association rather than proven. In a cohort of 69 confirmed ANDV-infected cases, salivary secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA) was significantly elevated (4.846 vs. 0.333 mg/mL in exposed-uninfected contacts), whereas mucins MUC7 and MUC5B were more frequently detected in exposed-but-not-infected household contacts, a cross-sectional finding whose direction of causation is unresolved. Total salivary sIgA is a non-specific marker of mucosal immune activation and has no pathogen specificity. Oral fluid IgM assays for Hantaan virus achieved 96.7% sensitivity and 94.9% specificity against serum reference, supporting further evaluation of non-invasive salivary surveillance. Clinically, severe sore throat persisting for 2 to 3 weeks and oropharyngeal edema are documented as early features of hantavirus infection. Thrombocytopenia, which may be profound during the oliguric phase of HFRS, confers significant oral hemorrhagic risk. Human hantavirus infection presents with clinically significant oral and salivary manifestations that are directly relevant to dental practitioners. Dental teams should be aware of the hemorrhagic risk in patients with thrombocytopenia, the aerosol risk in patients with HCPS, the theoretical risk of ANDV transmission via oral contact in endemic regions, and the emerging utility of salivary diagnostics. Recommendations for dental practice are extrapolated from medical, virological, and general infection control evidence, rather than from dental clinical research, and are identified as precautionary where that is the case.

full_text_sections.abstract: Abstract Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonotic pathogens responsible for 2 severe clinical syndromes in humans: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), affecting an estimated 150,000 to 200,000 individuals annually worldwide, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), characterized by fulminant pulmonary edema with case fatality rates approaching 40%. Although the systemic manifestations of hantavirus disease are well described, the oral and salivary dimensions of infection have received comparatively little attention in the dental literature. This review synthesizes current evidence on the virology, global epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, oral complications, diagnostic approaches, treatment options, and dental practice implications of human hantavirus infections. A narrative review with a structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar was conducted, supplemented by hand-searching and by consultation of the World Health Organization and European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control outbreak reporting. Particular attention was directed toward primary research on salivary immunity, oral fluid diagnostics, and salivary gland tropism. Andes virus (ANDV) antigen has been detected in secretory cells of human salivary glands, and ANDV uniquely resists the antiviral capacity of human saliva, providing a biologically plausible mechanism for its person-to-person transmissibility. Infectious virus has since been recovered from saliva and gingival crevicular fluid during acute infection, although a salivary route of transmission remains an epidemiological association rather than proven. In a cohort of 69 confirmed ANDV-infected cases, salivary secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA) was significantly elevated (4.846 vs. 0.333 mg/mL in exposed-uninfected contacts), whereas mucins MUC7 and MUC5B were more frequently detected in exposed-but-not-infected household contacts, a cross-sectional finding whose direction of causation is unresolved. Total salivary sIgA is a non-specific marker of mucosal immune activation and has no pathogen specificity. Oral fluid IgM assays for Hantaan virus achieved 96.7% sensitivity and 94.9% specificity against serum reference, supporting further evaluation of non-invasive salivary surveillance. Clinically, severe sore throat persisting for 2 to 3 weeks and oropharyngeal edema are documented as early features of hantavirus infection. Thrombocytopenia, which may be profound during the oliguric phase of HFRS, confers significant oral hemorrhagic risk. Human hantavirus infection presents with clinically significant oral and salivary manifestations that are directly relevant to dental practitioners. Dental teams should be aware of the hemorrhagic risk in patients with thrombocytopenia, the aerosol risk in patients with HCPS, the theoretical risk of ANDV transmission via oral contact in endemic regions, and the emerging utility of salivary diagnostics. Recommendations for dental practice are extrapolated from medical, virological, and general infection control evidence, rather than from dental clinical research, and are identified as precautionary where that is the case.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogens causing hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (≈150,000‑200,000 cases annually) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome with case‑fatality rates up to 40%, representing a significant public‑health threat.
analysis.methods: A narrative review was conducted using a structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and WHO/ECDC outbreak reports.
analysis.results: Andes virus antigen was detected in human salivary‑gland secretory cells and infectious virus recovered from saliva and gingival crevicular fluid; in a cohort of 69 confirmed cases salivary sIgA was markedly elevated (4.846 vs 0.333 mg/mL) compared with exposed uninfected contacts, and oral‑fluid IgM assays for Hantaan virus achieved 96.7 % sensitivity and 94.9 % specificity versus serum reference.
analysis.contribution: The review identifies oral and salivary manifestations (e.g., prolonged sore throat, thrombocytopenia‑related bleeding) relevant to dental practice and highlights potential transmission risks and the utility of non‑invasive salivary diagnostics.
analysis.limitations: Salivary transmission remains an epidemiological association rather than proven; practice recommendations are extrapolated and precautionary; the article is an abstract‑only narrative review.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and cardiopulmonary syndrome, affecting up to 200,000 people annually with high fatality. Methods: A narrative review used a structured search of major biomedical databases and WHO/ECDC reports. Results: Andes virus antigen was found in salivary glands and virus recovered from saliva; salivary sIgA was higher in 69 infected cases (4.846 vs 0.333 mg/mL) and oral‑fluid IgM testing showed 96.7 % sensitivity and 94.9 % specificity. Contribution: The work alerts dental teams to oral manifestations, hemorrhagic and aerosol risks, possible oral transmission, and the promise of salivary diagnostics. Limitations: Salivary transmission is only an association, recommendations are precautionary, and the paper is abstract‑only.

papers.title: Multi-host circulation and evolutionary dynamics of hantaviruses in small mammals in Southwestern China
papers.abstract: China represents a major hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS)-endemic region, where small mammals, particularly rodents, constitute the principal reservoir hosts. This study characterized HV diversity, RNA detection rate, host range, evolutionary history, and tissue distribution in 1 717 wild small mammals collected from Yunnan Province, China. HVs were detected in 47 animals, corresponding to an overall RNA detection rate of 2.74% (47/1 717, 95% CI: 1.97%–3.51%). At least five HV species or lineages were identified across 10 small mammal species, including Orthohantavirus luxiense (LUXV), Orthohantavirus fugongense (FUGV), Orthohantavirus seoulense (SEOV), Orthohantavirus caobangense (CBNV), and Thottimvirus sp. Host‐virus coevolutionary analysis suggested extensive interspecies transmission, with particularly strong support for phylogenetically inferred host‐switching events involving SEOV and FUGV. Preliminary analysis of tissue viral loads revealed that LUXV was widely distributed across various tissues and that significant differences in viral levels existed among tissues (χ2 = 27.500, P < 0.001). Collectively, these findings elucidate the genetic diversity and evolutionary dynamics of HVs in small mammals in Yunnan.

analysis.background: China is a major hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS)‑endemic region, where small mammals, especially rodents, serve as the principal reservoir hosts.
analysis.methods: The study screened 1,717 wild small mammals collected in Yunnan Province, China, characterizing hantavirus (HV) diversity, RNA detection rate, host range, evolutionary history and tissue distribution.
analysis.results: HV RNA was detected in 47 animals (overall detection rate 2.74%, 95% CI 1.97%–3.51%). At least five HV species/lineages (LUXV, FUGV, SEOV, CBNV, Thottimvirus sp.) were identified across 10 small‑mammal species. Co‑evolutionary analysis suggested extensive inter‑species transmission, with strong support for host‑switching events involving SEOV and FUGV. Preliminary tissue‑viral‑load analysis showed LUXV distributed across multiple tissues with significant differences among tissues (χ² = 27.500, P < 0.001).
analysis.contribution: These findings elucidate the genetic diversity and evolutionary dynamics of hantaviruses in Yunnan’s small mammals, providing data valuable for surveillance and zoonotic risk assessment.
analysis.limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: China is a major HFRS‑endemic region where rodents are principal reservoirs. Methods: The authors screened 1,717 wild small mammals from Yunnan Province, China, for hantavirus RNA, assessing diversity, host range, evolutionary history and tissue distribution. Results: Hantavirus RNA was detected in 47 animals (2.74%, 95% CI 1.97–3.51%). Five hantavirus species/lineages (LUXV, FUGV, SEOV, CBNV, Thottimvirus sp.) were found in 10 host species. Co‑evolutionary analysis indicated extensive inter‑species transmission, especially host‑switching between SEOV and FUGV. LUXV was present in multiple tissues with significant load differences (χ² = 27.5, P < 0.001). Contribution: The study clarifies the genetic diversity and evolutionary dynamics of hantaviruses in Yunnan’s small mammals, informing surveillance and zoonotic risk assessment. Limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

papers.title: Vaccines Against Hantavirus Infections: A Systematic Literature Review
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Hantaviruses infections are responsible for a hemorrhagic fever with renal and cardiopulmonary syndrome with case-fatality rates up to 50%. While inactivated vaccines are already available in China and South Korea, several additional candidate vaccines are under development. This systematic review summarizes the current clinical evidence on immunogenicity and short-term safety of vaccines targeting different hantavirus strains. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a systematic literature search was carried out to identify randomized and nonrandomized trials of any phase. Data were synthesized narratively within strata defined by vaccine platform, target virus, assay, immunogenicity and safety. Results: Ten trials on 961 adults were included: four single-arm trials on the inactivated vaccine and six early-phase DNA-vaccine trials. One month after last dose, the inactivated vaccine achieved neutralizing seropositivity by PRNT50 in 45.1% of the tested subjects after two priming doses and 55.7% after three, while the corresponding binding-antibody values measured by IFA were 87.3% and 95.7%. Among DNA vaccines, homologous responses reached 100% against HTNV and 83.3% against PUUV with monovalent constructs, whereas dual responses to the bivalent construct were registered in 33.3% and 77.8% of the subjects, when measured through PRNT50 and PsVNA50, respectively. One serious adverse event occurred, most likely unrelated to vaccination. Conclusions: No serious safety signal was identified, although safety remains insufficiently characterized. Measured immunogenicity depends as much on the assay as on the vaccine, and, in the absence of a validated correlate of protection, it cannot be read as a clinical benefit. Future research should prioritize validated correlates of protection and innovative trial designs adapted to low-incidence diseases.

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒导致肾综合征出血热与汉坦病毒心肺综合征,致死率高达50%,凸显了有效疫苗的必要性。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述聚焦于中国和韩国可获得的灭活疫苗以及新兴的 DNA 疫苗候选者,汇总了十项试验中通过中和和结合测定评估的免疫原性。
analysis_zh.current_state: 十项涉及961名成人的试验报告显示,灭活疫苗的中和抗体阳性率为45–56%,DNA 针对汉滩病毒的中和抗体可达100%,结合抗体率高,且仅出现一次严重不良事件,未见明显安全信号。
analysis_zh.gaps: 免疫原性结果因测定方法不同而异,缺乏经验证的保护相关指标,且安全数据仍有限。
analysis_zh.future_research: 未来研究应确立保护相关指标,并采用适用于低发病率汉坦病毒疾病的创新试验设计。

papers.title: Transmission timing and containment risk in human Andes virus outbreaks
papers.abstract: The 2026 multinational Andes virus (ANDV) outbreak linked to cruise-ship travel from Argentina triggered extensive contact tracing and quarantine. Whether intervention on this scale was necessary or sufficient depends on the risk of onward transmission, which can be difficult to estimate early in an outbreak. Using transmission-pair data from the 2018--2019 outbreak in Epuyen, Argentina, and a mechanistic model linking viral growth, symptom onset, and transmission, we estimated that 42.4% (95% CrI: 18.2-69.7\%) of transmission occurs before symptom onset and that the median incubation period is 18.5 days (95% CrI: 16.5-19.5). We simulated outbreaks under an Epuyen-calibrated estimate (R = 2.12, k = 0.316) and a pooled estimate from 15 prior ANDV investigations (R = 0.24, k = 0.39), with intervention beginning after two generations, as in the cruise-associated event. Under the higher-transmission scenario, missing 10% of exposed individuals or downstream contacts resulted in a 29.9% probability of continued spread and a 20.6% probability that at least 5,000 ultimately uninfected people would be quarantined. Under lower transmission, continued spread stayed below 8%. However, the risk of onward transmission could not be estimated precisely from the first several detected cases. These findings therefore support rapid, comprehensive contact tracing and quarantine after large international exposure events despite substantial costs.
